strapline: The budget meets its critics; 100,000 free pairs of spectacles; the 25 November march goes ahead; a treason bail ruling on Tuesday; and Zimba's bronze comes home

stories.title: Mobile money firms want talks, an economist names the winners and losers, and a former MP does the copper arithmetic: the 2027 budget meets its first day of scrutiny
stories.excerpt: A day after Situmbeko Musokotwane presented a K284.8 billion budget, the Mobile Money Association of Zambia said the higher transaction levies were decided without proper consultation and could undo gains in financial inclusion. Economist Lubinda Haabazoka said Social Cash Transfer households and farmers gain while consumers and mobile money users pay, and former Kamfinsa MP Christopher Kang'ombe calculated that copper output growing at its current pace reaches 1.3 million tonnes by 2031, not the three million the government is targeting.

image.label: The budget, day two
image.caption: Reaction to the 2027 budget turned on Saturday 7 November to the mobile money levy, the sugar excise and whether copper can triple by 2031.

body: A day after the Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, set out a K284.8 billion budget for 2027, the argument moved from the headline totals to who carries them. The Mobile Money Association of Zambia said on Saturday 7 November that the government had decided to raise levies on mobile money transactions without adequately consulting the industry, Zambia Monitor reported. The association's president and secretary general, Chris Sichende, told the Monitor in an interview that stakeholders had asked for meaningful engagement before any change affecting the sector, that higher levies would raise transaction costs for the individuals and businesses that use mobile money most, and that the government should weigh the effect on users before taking a final decision. The budget proposes raising mobile money levies across all transaction bands, with the stated aims of broadening the tax base, improving equity and raising more domestic revenue, according to the same report.

body.text: This has the potential to erode the gains made so far in terms of financial inclusion expansion.
body.attribution: Chris Sichende, president and secretary general of the Mobile Money Association of Zambia, in an interview published by Zambia Monitor on Saturday 7 November

body: Economist Lubinda Haabazoka's reading of the budget, reported by Zambia Monitor on Saturday, puts households on the Social Cash Transfer and farmers among the likely winners and consumers and mobile money users among the likely losers. Social Cash Transfer funding rises to K10.4 billion and the number of beneficiary households is projected to grow from 1.5 million this year to more than 1.6 million in 2027; education and health together receive K68.5 billion, about 24% of spending; school feeding nearly doubles from K523 million to K1 billion; agriculture, fisheries and livestock receive K22.7 billion, of which K9.1 billion is for the Farmer Input Support Programme; roads receive K18.1 billion; and the Constituency Development Fund rises from K6.2 billion to about K9 billion, roughly K40 million a constituency. Haabazoka's caveat, as the Monitor reported it, is that the higher taxes and levies could raise living costs and offset part of those gains, so that what any household actually receives depends on the services it uses, the markets it reaches and the taxes it pays.

The consumer measures are now being itemised. Mpelembe Media reported on Saturday that the budget proposes a specific excise duty of K1 a kilogram on refined sugar, an excise of 80 ngwee on each plastic bottle, a rise in excise on single-use plastics to 200%, the end of VAT zero-rating for energy-saving appliances alongside the rise in VAT from 16% to 16.5% on 1 January 2027, and the new 39.5% PAYE band on monthly earnings above K37,000. Mpelembe described the mobile money levy as doubled but gave no rates, and it carried two different figures for the duty on imported ceramic tiles, 40% in one passage and a rise from 15% to 25% for tiles from outside SADC and COMESA in another, without reconciling them. It also reported that the Fight Inequality Alliance and the Jesuit Centre for Theological Reflection say the K50 monthly increase in Social Cash Transfer payments does not keep pace with inflation. An explainer published by The Zambian Observer on Saturday put the standard transfer at K400 to K450 a month and the payment for households with a person with a disability at K600 to K650, noted that FISP is to move towards an agricultural loan scheme from 2027, and put debt service at K67.6 billion, close to a quarter of the budget.

The budget's growth story rests on mining, and that is where the sharpest arithmetic came from. Christopher Kang'ombe, the former Kamfinsa MP, wrote on his Facebook page, in remarks reported by Zambia Monitor on Saturday, that copper output is rising only about 4.5% a year, from 890,000 tonnes in 2025 to a projected 930,000 tonnes, and that at that pace Zambia reaches about 1.3 million tonnes by 2031, not the three million tonnes Musokotwane told Parliament remained within reach. Hitting the target, Kang'ombe said, would need average growth of about 26% a year from every producer, including NFCA. He went through them one by one: Mopani's Mufulira and Kitwe operations need big increases in 2027; Konkola Copper Mines is below expectations but could improve; First Quantum's Kansanshi and Trident lead but cannot close the gap alone; Barrick's Lumwana super pit should lift output though he doubted it would reach 26%; and Luanshya's contribution waits on the Shaft 28 project, while Lubambe lacks the material to make a difference.

Reuters, in a report carried by TimesLIVE on Saturday and by CNBC Africa on Friday, gave the government's side of the ledger: Musokotwane told Parliament on Friday 6 November that growth should stay around 5% in 2027, that the fiscal deficit is to fall to no more than 3% of GDP from 5.9% this year, and that copper output of 930,000 tonnes is expected in 2026, up from about 890,000 tonnes last year, under what he called a stable and predictable fiscal regime for mining companies. Reuters attributed this year's wider deficit to fuel tax cuts made to cushion households and businesses from the Iran war and to higher spending, including maize purchases for the national reserve, and noted that Zambia secured staff-level backing from the IMF in October for a new US$1.5 billion programme.

body.title: The measures under fire, as reported on Saturday
items: Mobile money: levies rise across all transaction bands; rates not itemised in the reports read (Zambia Monitor; Mpelembe)
Sugar: K1 per kilogram specific excise on refined sugar (Mpelembe)
Plastics: 80 ngwee per plastic bottle; single-use plastics excise to 200% (Mpelembe)
VAT: 16% to 16.5% from 1 January 2027; zero-rating ends for energy-saving appliances (Mpelembe)
PAYE: new 39.5% band above K37,000 a month (Zambia Monitor; Mpelembe; News Diggers)
Copper: 930,000 tonnes in 2026, 3 million targeted by 2031; Kang'ombe's projection 1.3 million (Zambia Monitor; Reuters)

body.confirmed: The association's objection and Sichende's quoted words (Zambia Monitor). Haabazoka's allocations: K10.4 billion for Social Cash Transfer, K68.5 billion for education and health, K1 billion for school feeding, K22.7 billion for agriculture including K9.1 billion for FISP, K18.1 billion for roads, CDF to about K9 billion (Zambia Monitor; the CDF, education and agriculture figures also in News Diggers and The Zambian Observer). The 890,000 to 930,000-tonne copper figures, the 5.9% to 3% deficit path, growth around 5% and the US$1.5 billion IMF programme (Reuters via TimesLIVE and CNBC Africa; Zambia Monitor). The sugar, plastics and VAT details (Mpelembe Media).
body.unverified: The actual mobile money levy rates and bands, which none of the reports read on Saturday itemised, and whether the levy is doubled as Mpelembe states. The duty on imported ceramic tiles, for which Mpelembe gives two conflicting figures. Kang'ombe's mine-by-mine assessment is his own analysis, posted on Facebook, and the government has not responded to it in any report found.

stories.title: 'Vision is freedom': Hichilema launches HH Vision 100,000, a programme to give free spectacles to learners, soldiers and the elderly, saying six million Zambians need them
stories.excerpt: President Hakainde Hichilema told the Zambia Ophthalmological Society's annual conference, in a virtual address, that 100,000 pairs of spectacles have been procured for Zambians who cannot afford them. He said one in five schoolchildren struggles to see the blackboard and nearly one in three adults has poor vision, and framed the scheme as social justice rather than charity. It was piloted at three Lusaka secondary schools and at Mikango Barracks.

image.label: HH Vision 100,000
image.caption: A programme to distribute 100,000 pairs of free spectacles was launched by President Hichilema in a virtual address to eye specialists meeting in Lusaka.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema has launched a programme to distribute 100,000 pairs of spectacles free of charge to Zambians who cannot pay for them, the Zambia Daily Mail reported on Saturday 7 November. The scheme, called HH Vision 100,000, is aimed at learners, older people, military personnel, persons with albinism and other vulnerable groups with poor eyesight, according to the Daily Mail and The Zambian Observer. The President announced it in a virtual address to the annual conference of the Zambia Ophthalmological Society in Lusaka, the Daily Mail reported, citing ZNBC.

The figures the President used set out the scale of the problem as he sees it. More than six million Zambians need spectacles, he said; one in five schoolchildren struggles to see the blackboard, and nearly one in three adults has poor vision. He described the initiative as a matter of social justice rather than charity, and said that people who cannot pay will be able to collect free spectacles at their nearest health facility, with schoolchildren and military personnel expected to be among the first to benefit, The Zambian Observer reported.

body.text: This programme is about giving back sight, restoring dignity and opening the doors of opportunity for our people.
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, in a virtual address to the Zambia Ophthalmological Society conference, as reported by the Zambia Daily Mail on Saturday 7 November

body: The programme was piloted in recent months at New Jack Secondary School in Chawama, Kabanana Secondary School in Mandevu and Chitanda Secondary School in Matero, and at a military base in Mikango, the Daily Mail reported. The Zambian Observer added Mikango Barracks, Mount Eugenia and the Shimabala area to the list of pilot sites. The President's argument for starting with learners and soldiers, in words the Daily Mail quoted, was that when learners see better they learn better, and when soldiers see better they serve better.

The launch lands in the week the government set out its 2027 spending plans. The budget presented on Friday 6 November allocates K30.3 billion to health and provides for the recruitment of 3,125 frontline health workers, according to News Diggers and Mpelembe Media. Neither of the reports on the spectacles programme said what the 100,000 pairs cost, who supplied them, how the first beneficiaries will be identified beyond the pilot sites, or over what period the distribution is to run.

body.title: HH Vision 100,000, as reported
items: 100,000 pairs of spectacles procured for people who cannot afford them (Zambia Daily Mail; The Zambian Observer)
Target groups: learners, older people, military personnel, persons with albinism and other vulnerable groups
Pilot sites: New Jack, Kabanana and Chitanda secondary schools in Lusaka; Mikango Barracks; Mount Eugenia; Shimabala
Access: free spectacles at the nearest health facility for those unable to pay (The Zambian Observer)
Not reported: cost, supplier, timetable and how eligibility will be assessed

stories.title: 'Why was the group supporting removal allowed to march?': civil society says it will go ahead on 25 November, as a UPND member abroad tells his party to end the term-limit debate
stories.excerpt: Transparency International Zambia, the Chapter One Foundation and the LCK Foundation say the government is being inconsistent in discouraging their 25 November procession in defence of presidential term limits after a petition to abolish the limits was presented to the National Assembly on 27 October and its supporters were allowed to march. The government's spokesman has called the debate imaginary. From the United States, a UPND member's Facebook live video urging the President to end the debate has been widely shared.

image.label: The 25 November march
image.caption: Civil society groups say their procession in defence of the two-term limit will go ahead on 25 November despite the government's advice to reconsider.

body: The civil society coalition planning a procession in defence of presidential term limits says it will not be talked out of it. News Diggers reported on Saturday 7 November that Transparency International Zambia has accused the government of inconsistency for discouraging the 25 November march while having allowed young people who support removing the limits to march to Parliament. Josiah Kalala, executive director of the Chapter One Foundation, said the organisations would demonstrate peacefully and within the law, and Linda Kasonde, executive director of the LCK Foundation, said the UPND government appeared to be deliberately preventing public gatherings, which she said undermines democracy, according to the Diggers report.

TI-Z's executive director, Maurice Nyambe, made the same point a day earlier. Daily Revelation Zambia reported on Friday 6 November that Nyambe said the advice from the Chief Government Spokesperson, Elvis Nkandu, to reconsider the march conflicted with the freedoms of expression and assembly in the Constitution, that it was not for a minister or the government to dictate how citizens express themselves, and that the coalition had given formal notice to the Zambia Police Service and expected it to act professionally.

body.text: Why was the group supporting the removal of term limits allowed to march while CSOs are being advised not to?
body.attribution: Maurice Nyambe, executive director of Transparency International Zambia, as quoted by Daily Revelation Zambia on Friday 6 November

body: Nkandu's position, as The Zambian Observer reported it on Friday, is that the third-term debate is an imaginary issue: neither President Hichilema nor the UPND's supreme organ has signalled any intention to extend term limits, free expression applies equally to supporters and opponents of constitutional change, and the President is focused on jobs, the cost of living and electricity generation. The Observer named the coalition as the Chapter One Foundation, Transparency International Zambia, Caritas Zambia, the Council of Churches in Zambia, the LCK Foundation and the NGO Coordinating Council, and said the trigger was a petition presented to the National Assembly on 27 October calling for the abolition of presidential term limits. In their joint statement of 3 November, reported by the Observer on 4 November, the groups said they disagreed with the petitioners but respected their right to speak, recalled the country's resistance to a third presidential term in 2001, and pointed out that the 2025 constitutional review consultations had recommended keeping the current limits.

body.text: A warning from inside the party

body: The debate is also dividing the ruling party's own supporters. The Zambian Observer reported on Saturday that Akashambatwa Masheke, a UPND member based in the United States, had urged the President in a widely shared Facebook live video to shut down the term-limit debate so the government could concentrate on the Grow Zambia Agenda. He warned that if the limits were removed and Hichilema then lost in 2031 the consequences would fall on the Zambezi region and on the President's family, said the party's parliamentary majority should not tempt it to amend the Constitution, cited the failed third-term bids of Frederick Chiluba and Edgar Lungu, and named the party's media director, Mark Simuuwe, among those whose conduct he said risked damaging the President's legacy. Hichilema was sworn in for a second and final term on 1 September, which under the current two-term limit makes him ineligible in 2031, the Observer noted. Masheke's remarks are his own, made in a personal video; the Observer's report carried no response from the party or from Simuuwe.

stories.title: 'Sacrifice is met with insinuation': Saviour Chishimba answers Charles Milupi's jibe at alliance partners who leave, as the Socialist Party explains why it is skipping by-elections
stories.excerpt: Charles Milupi, who chairs the UPND Alliance Council of Presidents, said that anyone leaving the alliance now that the President has finished his appointments would show they joined only for a position; only two alliance leaders, Milupi and Felix Mutati, are in Cabinet. UPP president Saviour Chishimba replied that he was one of six people at the alliance's founding meeting in 2017 and that Milupi has been persistently inaccessible. Separately, the Socialist Party says it is skipping by-elections to rebuild after a poor August.

image.label: Inside the UPND Alliance
image.caption: A remark by the alliance chairman about partners who leave after the appointments has drawn a sharp written reply from one of the alliance's founders.

body: Charles Milupi, Minister of Transport and Logistics and chairperson of the UPND Alliance Council of Presidents, said in an interview on Wednesday that any member who leaves the alliance now, after President Hakainde Hichilema has completed his appointments, would be showing that they had joined only to seek a position, News Diggers reported on Saturday 7 November. The President recently appointed 30 Cabinet ministers and 10 provincial ministers, and only two members of the Council of Presidents were among them: Milupi himself, and the MDC leader Felix Mutati, who kept his post as Minister of Technology and Science, according to the Diggers report, which The Zambian Observer republished.

The reply came within hours. In a statement published by The Zambian Observer late on Saturday under the heading that political alliances cannot flourish where consultation is absent and sacrifice is met with insinuation, Saviour Chishimba, president of the United Progressive People, objected to the remarks "if these remarks have indeed been accurately attributed". He said he was one of six people at the alliance's inaugural meeting at Community House in 2017, alongside Hichilema, Geoffrey Bwalya Mwamba, the late Mike Mulongoti, Milupi and Nevers Mumba; that Milupi had been persistently inaccessible to him as alliance chairperson, with calls and messages unanswered, a complaint he said he raised at the official opening of Parliament; and that he and others had carried heavy personal costs in the 2026 campaign from which they were still recovering. He called for an alliance chairperson who is accessible and whose public statements reinforce the dignity of members. The statement is Chishimba's own account; no response from Milupi had been reported by Sunday morning.

body.text: Hon. Milupi has remained persistently inaccessible to me in his capacity as Alliance Chairperson.
body.attribution: Saviour Chishimba, president of the United Progressive People, in a statement published by The Zambian Observer on Saturday 7 November

body: On the other side of the aisle, the Socialist Party has explained why it has not fielded a single candidate in the by-elections held since August. Its general secretary, Cosmas Musumali, told News Diggers in an interview published on Saturday that the party is concentrating on rebuilding its structures, that by-elections are expensive and the party has had to ask whether contesting them is economically viable given how weak those structures are, and that the decision came out of a review the party began immediately after what he called its very poor performance in the August general election.

The ruling party, meanwhile, spent the week answering its foreign critic. Gertrude Imenda, a UPND proportional-representation MP, said in an interview on Wednesday that the Patriotic Front administration had been more dictatorial than the present government, told the former Botswana president Ian Khama to attend to his own country's affairs, and said politicians should not escape punishment for offences they have committed, News Diggers reported on Saturday. Her remarks followed a statement on Monday by the Tonse Alliance chairman, Sakwiba Sikota, that Khama's description of Hichilema as Africa's newest dictator reflected growing concern about democracy and human rights in Zambia, according to the same report.

stories.title: Nearly three in four farmers have their inputs, and some are selling them: the ministry warns against resale and shared codes as the budget plans a move from FISP to farm loans
stories.excerpt: As of Friday 6 November, 742,447 farmers, or 72.47% of the 1,024,434 targeted, had redeemed their inputs under the 2026/27 Farmer Input Support Programme, the Ministry of Agriculture said on Saturday. It also said it had received reports from several districts of farmers selling redeemed inputs to agro-dealers and sharing their e-voucher codes with cooperative leaders, and warned both farmers and dealers of action. The 2027 budget gives FISP K9.1 billion within K22.7 billion for agriculture.

image.label: FISP 2026/27
image.caption: Nearly three quarters of targeted farmers have collected their inputs, but the Ministry of Agriculture says some are being sold on.

body: The Ministry of Agriculture says 742,447 farmers had redeemed their inputs under the 2026/2027 Farmer Input Support Programme by Friday 6 November, 72.47% of the 1,024,434 beneficiaries targeted across the country, Zambia Monitor reported on Saturday 7 November. The figure came in a statement issued in Lusaka on Saturday by the ministry's principal public relations officer, Bhalewa Zyuulu, and it came with a complaint: the ministry has received reports from several districts that some farmers are selling the inputs they have just collected to agro-dealers and others, which Zyuulu said undermines the programme's purpose of raising production, productivity and national food security.

The statement, as the Monitor reported it, also described farmers sharing their e-voucher codes with cooperative leaders and intermediaries. Zyuulu advised farmers to protect their codes and personal identification details and to collect inputs individually from authorised agro-dealers, warning that anyone who hands a code to a third party risks unauthorised transactions and the loss of their entitlement. Accredited agro-dealers were told not to buy back, receive or facilitate the resale of farmers' inputs and to follow the programme's operational guidelines, and the ministry said anyone undermining the programme risked action under those guidelines.

The pace of redemption has picked up sharply since the season opened. At the start of September MUVI TV reported ministry figures of 270,523 farmers issued with redemption codes and 51,052 who had collected inputs, together with the same advice that codes should never be shared and that no agro-dealer may deny an eligible farmer access to inputs. Two months later the ministry's count stands at three quarters of the target, with the planting rains approaching.

body.text: What the budget does with FISP

body: The programme's future shape was set out in Friday's budget. The Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, allocated K22.7 billion to agriculture, fisheries and livestock for 2027, of which K9.1 billion is for FISP and K100 million for beef compartments in support of a target of US$1 billion a year in beef exports, Zambia Monitor reported. He listed eight Grow Zambia Agenda targets that bear on the sector, among them 10 million tonnes of maize, three million tonnes of soya beans, one million tonnes each of wheat and sugar and the beef export goal, and announced a farm block development agency to coordinate infrastructure and investment, a review of agricultural land policy favouring land near water, roads, rail and power, six more mechanisation centres in each district by 2031 on top of the existing 125, irrigation of at least 500,000 hectares by 2031, and commencement orders in 2027 for the Food Reserve Agency Act, the Agricultural Marketing Act and the Agricultural Credit and Warehouse Receipts Act, all passed in 2026. An explainer in The Zambian Observer on Saturday reported that FISP itself is planned to shift towards an agricultural loan scheme beginning in 2027, and economist Lubinda Haabazoka counted farmers among the budget's likely winners, according to Zambia Monitor.

stories.title: 'The State does not want it heard': a defence lawyer says the prosecution fears the 18 treason accused would be freed if their bail plea is argued, before Tuesday's ruling
stories.excerpt: Milner Katolo, one of the lawyers for Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others, says the State has openly admitted it does not want their constitutional bail application heard, and that the substantive hearing will start at once if the court overrules the State's objection on Tuesday 10 November. The State argued on Thursday that the application was wrongly before the court. In Solwezi, the Subordinate Court has sent the separate sedition case to Lusaka, and Zulu has asked to represent himself.

image.label: Tuesday's ruling
image.caption: The Lusaka High Court is to rule on 10 November on whether it can hear the constitutional bail application of 18 accused in the treason case.

body: The lawyers for the 18 people held on treason and terrorism-related charges, among them the 2026 presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu, say the State is trying to stop their bail application from being heard at all. News Diggers reported on Saturday 7 November that Milner Katolo, one of the defence lawyers, said the State had openly admitted that it did not want the constitutional bail application for the 18 heard, and that its fear was that the court would release them if it did. The Lusaka High Court is due to rule on Tuesday 10 November on whether it has jurisdiction to hear the application; Katolo said that if the State's preliminary objection is overruled the substantive bail hearing will proceed immediately, according to the Diggers report. The State raised the preliminary issue on Thursday 5 November, arguing that the application was wrongly before the court. The Diggers report is behind a paywall and the State's reasoning was not visible in the part published openly, so its full argument is not set out here.

The applicants have been brought to court from Mukobeko Maximum Security Correctional Facility for each sitting, Zambia Monitor reported on 29 October, when a three-judge panel of Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga warned that there would be no further adjournments after the Attorney General, Mulilo Kabesha, asked for more time to study the applicants' 32-paragraph affidavit and skeleton arguments. At that hearing Katolo argued that paragraph 59 of the National Prosecutions Authority's own manual recognises constitutional bail where trial proceedings are delayed, and raised concerns about the health of one of the applicants, who he said had missed appointments with a specialist abroad, according to the Monitor.

body.text: Solwezi sends the sedition case to Lusaka

body: The separate sedition case against Mundubile and Zulu is moving as well. Zambia Monitor reported on Friday 6 November that the Subordinate Court in Solwezi had ruled that Lusaka is the proper territorial forum, after examining sections 69, 70 and 72 of the Criminal Procedure Code and rejecting the argument that a livestream accessible across the country was enough to found jurisdiction in Solwezi. The court said that the mere assertion that the livestream was accessible nationwide did not, without more, establish the necessary connection, and declined to hear the matter there. The Monitor also reported that Zulu, a lawyer and vice-president of the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance, has asked the Lusaka High Court for leave to conduct his own case in the constitutional bail application, drawing a comparison in the report with the 1975 case of Shamwana v The People.
All 18 remain accused persons who have not been tried, and the bail application is about their detention pending trial, not about the charges themselves.

body.confirmed: The jurisdiction ruling is set for Tuesday 10 November and the State raised a preliminary objection on Thursday 5 November (News Diggers). The three-judge panel, the 18 applicants held at Mukobeko and the Attorney General's earlier request for time (Zambia Monitor, 29 October). The Solwezi Subordinate Court's ruling that the sedition case belongs in Lusaka, and Zulu's request to represent himself (Zambia Monitor, 6 November).
body.unverified: Katolo's characterisation of the State's position, that it does not want the application heard and fears the accused would be released, is the defence's account; the State's full argument was not visible in the report read and no response from the National Prosecutions Authority or the Attorney General to Katolo's remarks had been reported by Sunday morning. No date has been reported for the sedition case to begin in Lusaka.

stories.title: Bronze comes home: Elisha Zimba, 17, is welcomed at Kenneth Kaunda International after his judo medal in Dakar, as Grizzly Mining backs the women's sevens with US$25,000
stories.excerpt: Elisha Zimba, who won bronze in the boys' 55 kilogram judo at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games on 1 November, was met at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport by officials of the National Olympic Committee, the National Sports Council, OYDC Zambia and the Judo Association. NOCZ president Alfred Foloko, in remarks read for him, congratulated Zimba and urged companies to back young athletes before, not after, they win. Grizzly Mining has given the Zambia Rugby Union US$25,000 for the women's sevens trip to Nairobi.

image.label: Zimba's bronze
image.caption: Zambia's Youth Olympic judo medallist was welcomed home at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on Saturday 7 November.

body: Elisha Zimba came home on Saturday 7 November to what News Diggers called a thunderous welcome at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport, six days after winning bronze in the boys' 55 kilogram judo at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Waiting for him, the Diggers report said, were Mwape Zulu, a board member of the National Olympic Committee of Zambia, Sombwa Musunsa, chief executive of the National Sports Council of Zambia, Benjamin Tembo, acting chief executive of OYDC Zambia, and Mabvuto Ng'uni, general secretary of the Judo Association of Zambia.

Zulu spoke on behalf of the NOCZ president, Alfred Foloko, who congratulated Zimba for making the nation proud and used the occasion to press the corporate sector to invest in young athletes early rather than waiting until they have already succeeded, according to News Diggers. The report, which is behind a paywall, did not carry Zimba's own words in the part published openly.

The international judo database JudoInside, which lists Zimba as born on 27 December 2008, records his Dakar campaign on 1 November 2026 in the under-55 kilogram class: a win over Sangay Thinley of Bhutan, a quarter-final defeat by Tugskhuslen Tungalag of Mongolia, a further win over Thinley on the way back through the draw, and victory over Mutaz Hebah of Saudi Arabia in the bout for third place. News Diggers described the medal as historic, and it is the only result JudoInside holds for him, which says something about how new the 17-year-old is to the international circuit.

The call for early corporate backing was answered the same day in another code. Grizzly Mining Limited has committed US$25,000 to the Zambia Rugby Union to cover the preparation, travel and participation of the national women's rugby sevens team at the Rugby Africa Women's Sevens in Nairobi, News Diggers reported on Saturday. In a statement quoted by the Diggers, the company said it believes meaningful corporate support goes beyond business and that its backing reflects a commitment to women in sport and to the talent, determination and resilience of female athletes. The dates of the Nairobi tournament were not given in the part of the report published openly.

stories.title: Kangwa back for Bujumbura but not Ndola, Daka goes the distance for Hamburg, and Nkana visit winless Napsa on Sunday: the week before the Burundi double-header
stories.excerpt: Klings Kangwa has served the four-match ban CAF imposed after his stoppage-time red card against Morocco at AFCON 2025 and is available for the return leg in Bujumbura on 17 November, though he still misses the home qualifier at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on 13 November. Patson Daka played all 90 minutes as Hamburg beat Borussia Mönchengladbach 3–1 on Friday. In the Super League, Nkana travel to Reiz Arena on Sunday to face a Napsa Stars side still without a win.

image.label: The Burundi week
image.caption: Zambia host Burundi in Ndola on 13 November and travel to Bujumbura four days later in Group I of the AFCON 2027 qualifiers.

body: Klings Kangwa will be back for Zambia's second Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Burundi, but not the first. ZamFoot reported on Saturday 7 November that, according to the Confederation of African Football, the midfielder has completed the four-match suspension that followed his sending-off in stoppage time of Zambia's 3–0 defeat by Morocco at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, an incident that came after he had already been substituted for Given Kalusa in the 79th minute and that CAF treated more severely because of an altercation with the match official during and after it. He therefore misses the home leg at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Friday 13 November and is eligible for the return in Bujumbura on Tuesday 17 November.

The standings make the two games matter. ZamFoot put Zambia second in Group I with three points from two matches, one behind Algeria, with Togo also on three and Burundi bottom on one. The tournament the group feeds, branded AFCON Pamoja 2027, is to be co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania from 19 June to 17 July 2027.

One of the forwards Zambia will hope to have fit arrives in form, or at least in rhythm. Patson Daka started and played the full 90 minutes as Hamburger SV beat Borussia Mönchengladbach 3–1 at the Volksparkstadion on Friday night in the Bundesliga's ninth round, ZamFoot reported. He did not score: in the eighth minute he pounced on a misplaced back-pass but was denied one-on-one by the Gladbach goalkeeper Moritz Nicolas. Miro Muheim then struck from about 30 metres three minutes later, Joe Scally equalised in the 44th minute, Ko Itakura was sent off for a second booking in the 49th, and Fabio Baldé Nandja in the 60th minute and Albert Grønbæk ten minutes after that won it for Merlin Polzin's side. ZamFoot's assessment was that the full 90 minutes was what Daka needed to keep his place in the Hamburg attack.

At home, the Super League squeezes in a rescheduled match before the international break takes hold. Nkana travel to Reiz Arena in Lusaka on Sunday 8 November for a Week 3 fixture against Napsa Stars, the first of three consecutive away games, with a chance to press their claim on the top of Stream A after a 1–0 midweek win over Kansanshi Dynamos, News Diggers reported on Saturday. Napsa, ninth in the table, are still looking for a first win of the season after losing 1–0 to the champions Power Dynamos in their last outing; their assistant coach, Zeddy Saileti, acknowledged the difficulties facing his young side in remarks the Diggers report began to quote before its paywall.

stories.title: Three nights of Chinese cinema in Lusaka: The Wandering Earth opens a four-film festival that Beijing's embassy frames around 70 years of China–Africa relations
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Chinese Film Festival ran in Lusaka from 5 to 7 November with four films, opening with the science-fiction epic The Wandering Earth. China's ambassador, Han Jing, and the Minister of Culture and Arts, Chris Chibuye, spoke at the opening ceremony, according to a statement issued by the Chinese embassy through APO Group, the only account of the event found; the minister argued that cultural and creative industries can create jobs and asked for cooperation on infrastructure, skills and financing.

image.label: Chinese film festival
image.caption: Four Chinese films were screened in Lusaka over three days, opening on 5 November with The Wandering Earth.

body: Lusaka has had three nights of Chinese cinema. The Zambia Chinese Film Festival opened on Wednesday 5 November and ran until Saturday 7 November with four films: the science-fiction epic The Wandering Earth, The Shadow's Edge, Dear You and the animated Boonie Bears: Future Reborn, according to a statement from the Embassy of the People's Republic of China in Zambia, distributed by APO Group and published by Pan African Visions on Friday 6 November. Guests at the opening ceremony watched The Wandering Earth after the speeches.

The ambassador, Han Jing, told the opening that the language of film crosses national borders and bridges cultural differences, and placed the festival within the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and African states and what Beijing has designated the 2026 China–Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges, the statement said. He called for more regular cultural exchange and for partnership in all sectors in support of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The Minister of Culture and Arts, Chris Chibuye, used the platform to make an economic case for culture. According to the embassy's account, he said films strengthen the friendship between the two countries, argued that developing cultural and creative industries can create jobs, stimulate business and open new avenues of growth, and asked for cooperation on local infrastructure, skills training and access to financing for the sector. The Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet, Siazongo Siakalenge, also attended, the statement said.

A caution on sourcing: the account above rests on a single statement issued by the Chinese embassy and republished by several syndication sites, and the embassy's text reports both speakers in indirect speech. No report of the festival by an independent Zambian outlet was found by Sunday morning, and the statement did not name the screening venues, say how many people attended, or say whether admission was free. Readers who went will know more about the rooms and the crowds than the embassy's text records.

analysis.title: The mobile money levy: easy to collect, hard to defend, and still not itemised
analysis.body: Of all the measures in Friday's budget, the rise in mobile money levies is the one most Zambians will feel first, and it is the one whose details are least visible. The government's case, as reported, is that the levy broadens the tax base, improves equity and raises revenue from a channel through which a great deal of money now moves outside the banks. The industry's case is that the levy is a charge on the poorest users of the financial system, that it raises the cost of every small transfer and that it risks pushing people back to cash, undoing the inclusion gains the government itself celebrates. Both can be true at once. What is missing is the arithmetic: none of the reports read on Saturday gave the new rates or bands, and one outlet's description of the levy as doubled has not been confirmed elsewhere. Two things to watch: the text of the revenue bills when they reach Parliament's committees, and whether the Ministry of Finance publishes a band-by-band table. Until it does, both the association's warning and the government's reassurance are arguments about a number nobody outside the ministry has seen.

analysis.title: A march about a bill that does not exist: what 25 November actually tests
analysis.body: The government's objection to the 25 November procession is that there is nothing to march against: no bill, no party resolution, no presidential statement. The organisers' answer is that a petition to abolish term limits was received by the National Assembly on 27 October, that its supporters were allowed to walk to Parliament, and that the only way to show the other view exists is to walk too. Both positions are defensible, and the dispute is less about term limits than about who may gather in public and when. That is why the first real test comes before the march. The coalition has given notice to the police; whether the police acknowledge it, impose conditions or invoke the Public Order Act will say more about the state of assembly rights than any speech on the day. The second test is inside the ruling party. A UPND member's widely shared plea to shut the debate down shows the question is not simply government against civil society. What to watch: the police response to the notice, any statement from the UPND's own organs, and whether the 27 October petition is ever tabled as a motion.

analysis.title: Tuesday's ruling is about jurisdiction, not liberty, and that is the point
analysis.body: When the Lusaka High Court rules on Tuesday 10 November, it will not be deciding whether 18 people accused of treason should be released. It will be deciding whether it can hear the question at all. The State's preliminary objection, raised on Thursday, is that the constitutional bail application is wrongly before the court; the defence's reply is that the objection is a device to keep the application from being argued, and the defence has also argued that the prosecution's own manual contemplates constitutional bail where a trial is delayed. If the objection is sustained, the application falls away and the applicants' next step has not been reported. If it is overruled, the defence says the substantive hearing starts at once, with the State's readiness then the issue. Either way, the applicants remain at Mukobeko with no trial date set, since the court said in October that dates would follow its ruling on bail, and the Solwezi court's decision to send the separate sedition case to Lusaka adds a second file to the same calendar. What to watch: the ruling itself, the reasons given for it, and whether any trial date follows.
